title: The passcode in the response body
dek: DW's German-learning platform returned the email verification code in the API response — the same code that was meant to prove you could read the inbox. Found and reported in 2025, acknowledged by DW.
body: Email verification is there to prove one thing: that whoever is signing up can read mail sent to that address. It works only because the code travels by a channel the person does not otherwise control — the inbox. The moment the code appears on the sign-up channel itself, the proof is gone.

I was learning German on DW's platform, and one day I turned the same curiosity on the site itself. I put the login and registration flow through Burp Suite, which lets you read what the server actually sends the browser rather than what the page chooses to show. The response to the registration request carried the verification code as a field. The page never displayed it. The browser was just expected to ignore it.

Because the code was in the response, anyone watching the response had it. So any address could be verified without ever opening its inbox — including addresses that were not mine, such as an admin@ address on DW's own domain. This was not a leak of existing accounts. It was a way around the check that verification was supposed to be, on an address belonging to someone else. Anywhere a verified address is later trusted as identity, that trust was no longer safe.

The fix is not complicated: the code never leaves the server. The response says only whether a mail was sent. Verification is a second request that carries the code the user typed, and the server compares it against a stored copy with an expiry and a limit on tries. The user is told the result, never the secret.

Timeline: found and written up in 2025, and reported to DW's security contact with the request, the response field, and the impact stated plainly. It was acknowledged with thanks. There was no bug bounty running, so that was the end of it — and that is worth saying, because a disclosure is no less real for being unpaid. I have not gone back to confirm the fix, so I am not claiming one.

What I took from it: read the whole response, not the rendered page. A field the interface ignores is still a field the server chose to send, and the browser is the last place you should keep a secret. I write my own verification flows differently because of this one. No exploit steps beyond what is written here are published.
